response:
OLS with cluster-robust standard errors (CRSE) is a reasonable starting point, but your data structure raises several issues that make multilevel modeling (MLM) the more principled choice here.

The structure you have is three-level nested: measurements (level 1) are nested within students (level 2), who are nested within schools (level 3). OLS with CRSE, even if you cluster at the school level, collapses this hierarchy and doesn't properly partition variance across the three levels. You'd be ignoring the student-level clustering when estimating residuals, and you won't get estimates of between-student versus between-school variance components, which matter for understanding where the intervention effect operates.

The bigger concern is that 25 schools is a small number of level-3 units. For school-level inference — which is exactly what you want, since the intervention is at the school level — standard asymptotic justifications for CRSE require many clusters. The common rule of thumb is at least 30–50 clusters for CRSE to behave well; at 25, the sandwich estimator can be badly biased downward, leading to anti-conservative inference. This is a known problem: Cameron & Miller (2015) and others document that CRSE with few clusters produces undersized standard errors and inflated t-statistics. You could apply bias-corrected CRSE (e.g., CR2/HC3 variants, the 'BRL' correction from Pustejovsky & Tipton), but you're still pushing the limits of the asymptotic framework.

MLM is the preferred approach here. A three-level mixed model — with random intercepts (and possibly slopes) for students and schools — correctly accounts for the nested structure, allows you to model the intervention as a fixed effect at the school level, and gives you valid likelihood-based inference on variance components. With 1500 students across 25 schools (60 students per school on average) and 3 time points, you have reasonable level-1 and level-2 sample sizes; the weakness is at level 3 (25 schools).

With only 25 level-3 units, standard REML-based MLM also has limitations. The number of schools is too small for reliable asymptotic inference on school-level fixed effects using default t/z tests. You should apply Kenward-Roger (KR) degrees-of-freedom corrections (available in lme4 + pbkrtest, or SAS PROC MIXED), which adjust standard errors and use approximate finite-sample t-distributions rather than z-tests. Alternatively, Bayesian estimation (e.g., brms/Stan) is well-suited here: it doesn't rely on asymptotic normality for the level-3 parameters, handles small cluster counts gracefully, and lets you place weakly informative priors on variance components to stabilize estimates when data are sparse at the top level.

Summary: Don't rely on plain OLS+CRSE — the three-level structure and small number of schools both work against it. Use a three-level MLM with KR corrections or Bayesian estimation. If you insist on CRSE as a robustness check, use CR2-corrected standard errors, but treat it as secondary to the MLM results.
